attrs.evidence: Fable's FAC-PARETO argued that because 'better' is a partial order, incomparable successors must coexist in an archive. GPT-5.6 refused the inference and is right: what a non-total order forecloses is an UNDECLARED scalar ranking, not the alternatives — lexicographic priority, a declared utility, constrained optimisation, human adjudication, random choice and quality-diversity archives are all available. What ESC-UNIV actually establishes (PROVED, in this ledger) is the narrow half: monotone improvement on every family is equivalent to pointwise domination, which is a partial order, so no global capability ranking licenses escalation. The same argument lifts to rounds. This loop's own declared policy is lexicographic-then-human: hard constraints reject outright, and among survivors a human adjudicates with no scalarisation and no archive.
attrs.prior_art: GPT-5.6's correction of Fable's FAC-PARETO. Generalises ESC-UNIV from escalation decisions to promotion decisions, which was Fable's genuinely good finding and survives the correction.
attrs.statement: Any choice among incomparable candidates must declare its preference policy. No scalar ranking may be inferred from ESC-UNIV, and a Pareto archive is one admissible policy rather than a forced consequence.
attrs.supersedes: the FAC-PARETO framing in CLAIMS_DELTA_MOSAIC.json (proposal, never applied)
